analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary cutoff for overtime pay for salaried workers and updates it annually.
analysis.headline: A bill to make millions of salaried workers earning under $75,000 eligible for overtime pay has 34 Democratic cosponsors but has sat untouched in committee since its May 2026 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, salaried workers classified as executive, administrative, or professional can be denied overtime no matter how many hours they work, as long as they earn above a low salary cutoff. This bill raises that cutoff from about $35,600 to $45,000 immediately after passage, then steps it up to $75,000 by 2029, after which it rises automatically with national wages. It also caps the amount of hands-on work a so-called executive can do and still be denied overtime, and requires the government to publish the wage data used to set the cutoff.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers who are currently classified as exempt and denied overtime but earn between roughly $35,600 and $75,000. Millions of assistant managers, shift leads, office coordinators, and early-career professionals in that range would become eligible for time-and-a-half pay past 40 hours a week, or their employers would have to raise their salaries or cap their hours. The automatic annual updates also protect future workers, since the cutoff would rise with wages instead of eroding for decades as it has in the past.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a federal salary floor for overtime exemption at $45,000 when the act takes effect, rising to $55,000 in 2027, $65,000 in 2028, and $75,000 in 2029, after which the cutoff is tied to the 55th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally.
Requires the Labor Department to update the salary threshold every year automatically, so the cutoff rises with wages instead of staying frozen for years as the current one has.

Cuts the share of non-supervisory work an 'executive' can perform and still be denied overtime from 40% (in retail and service establishments) to no more than 20%, tightening a loophole that lets employers classify working shift managers as exempt.

Requires the Labor Department to publish each new threshold in the Federal Register at least 60 days before it takes effect, and requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish quarterly data on weekly salaried earnings so workers and employers can see how the cutoff is set.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of salaried workers. Businesses would have to pay overtime to newly covered employees, raise their salaries above the threshold, or limit their hours. The cost falls hardest on retail, restaurant, and hotel chains that rely on salaried shift managers, on employers in lower-wage regions where $75,000 is far above local salaries, and on small businesses and nonprofits with lean salaried staff. Some workers could also see employers restructure jobs, converting salaried posts to hourly ones or cutting scheduled hours to avoid overtime bills.

drawbacks.text: The cost lands on employers, including small businesses and nonprofits, that would owe overtime or higher salaries to workers earning up to $75,000 by 2029; some would respond by converting salaried jobs to hourly ones, cutting hours, or hiring fewer people.

A single national threshold of $75,000 is a large jump in low-wage regions, where it exceeds typical salaried pay and could push employers to restructure management jobs rather than raise wages to that level.

Tightening the duties test so 'executives' may spend no more than 20% of their time on hands-on work removes a training path some workers use, since working-manager roles in retail and food service have traditionally been a step toward higher-paying management.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains to workers are substantial and the design is sound: the stepped schedule gives employers over three years to adjust, and tying the cutoff to the 55th percentile of salaried wages prevents the slow erosion that left the current threshold so low. The real cost is the adjustment burden on employers, especially small businesses, nonprofits, and firms in low-wage regions, and there is a genuine risk that some workers see hours cut or jobs converted to hourly rather than getting overtime. On balance, the bill is a straightforward wage-floor increase for a group of workers the current rules leave out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2026 on May 15, 2026, with 22 original Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day.
The bill has attracted 34 cosponsors, all of them Democrats; no Republican has signed on.
Since the referral in May 2026, the committee has held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, and the full House has not considered it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, employers of salaried workers, who face no new overtime obligations while the bill sits without committee action. Workers earning between roughly $35,600 and $75,000 gain nothing unless it moves.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors are Democrats and none are Republicans, and the bill sits in the Republican-led Education and Workforce Committee with no action taken.

industries.note: These chains commonly classify salaried shift and store managers as exempt 'executives' and may assign them up to 40% of their time to nonexempt work like running registers or stocking shelves. The bill cuts that allowance to 20% and requires salaries up to $75,000 by 2029, so chains would owe overtime or pay significantly more for the same managers.

industries.industry: Salaried white-collar employers (finance, insurance, healthcare administration, tech, nonprofits)
industries.note: Any employer with salaried staff earning between roughly $35,600 and $75,000 who currently work more than 40 hours without overtime would owe time-and-a-half, higher salaries, or shorter hours. Small businesses and nonprofits with lean salaried staff bear a disproportionate share of the adjustment.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action more than a month after introduction, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or a floor vote. Its most probable end is dying quietly in committee when this Congress adjourns in January 2027, the same fate that met similar overtime bills introduced by Democrats in past Congresses.
